title: The Sermon Without God: Ethical Culture, the Free Kindergarten, and the Children in the Mills
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Rabbi's House: Alzey to Twelfth Street

stops.name: Worms, the Heiliger Sand: the grandfather in the Rabbinental
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the burial rests on a single 2014 dedication text at aeu.org that now returns 404, and the month and day are placeholders
stops.campa: At Worms lies the Heiliger Sand, the oldest surviving Jewish cemetery in Europe, its rabbis gathered in the plot the Jews of the town call the Rabbinental. Isaak Adler, Torah scholar, dead in 1822, is said to lie there. The German account of the cemetery does not list him among its notable graves, and the speech that names him has gone off the web. Twenty miles west, at Alzey, his son Samuel holds the rabbinate, and the grandson Isaak never meets is born there twenty-nine years after this burial.
suggested_refs: The Rabbinental of the Heiliger Sand, Worms
sources: Gerhard Holzer, dedication speech, American Ethical Union (aeu.org), 2014, now unreachable

stops.name: Alzey, the corner house of Schlossgasse and Amtsgasse: a second son
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the corner house where Schlossgasse meets Amtsgasse, in the Rhenish Hessian town of Alzey, a second son is born to Rabbi Samuel Adler and Henrietta Frankfurter. The father leads the Jewish community of the town and stands in a line of scholars reaching back down the Rhine to Worms. The child is named Felix. Alzey will keep almost no memory of him: a century and a half later a German admirer will stand in this street and report that the founder of a New York movement is scarcely known in the town where he was born.
suggested_refs: The birth house at the corner of Schlossgasse and Amtsgasse, Alzey
The Samuel Adler memorial on Hospitalstrasse, Alzey
sources: Gerhard Holzer, dedication speech, American Ethical Union (aeu.org), 2014

stops.name: Le Havre, the port that no source names
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the emigration is attested, the port is not; no source consulted names the quay
stops.campa: Samuel Adler is called to Temple Emanu-El in New York and the household leaves Germany in February, the boy five and a half years old. Which quay they walk down is nowhere recorded. Le Havre and Bremen carry the Rhineland out of Europe in these decades, and this pin marks the likelier of the two rather than a documented fact. What the crossing settles is not in doubt: the son of a Hessian rabbi will grow up American, and the pulpit waiting at the far end is the one he is expected to inherit.
suggested_refs: Standard 1850s German Jewish emigration routes out of the Rhineland
sources: Gerhard Holzer, dedication speech, American Ethical Union, 2014 (February 1857, age five and a half)

stops.name: Temple Emanu-El, Twelfth Street: the head rabbi's household
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the Twelfth Street building; the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: Emanu-El is housed on East Twelfth Street when the Adlers arrive, and will not move to its Fifth Avenue synagogue until 1868. Samuel Adler takes the pulpit and holds it seventeen years as the leading Reform rabbi of the city. Felix grows up inside that authority: German at home, English in the street, the liturgy the ordinary furniture of the house. The congregation that hears the father every week of its life is the congregation that will hear the son exactly once.
suggested_refs: The Twelfth Street synagogue of Congregation Emanu-El, occupied 1854 to 1868

stops.name: Columbia College, Forty-ninth Street and Madison: highest honors
stops.date_confidence: attested for the graduation; month and day not given in any source consulted
stops.campa: He is schooled in the public and private classrooms of the city, Columbia Grammar among them, though nothing consulted says which building the grammar school occupied in the 1860s. At Columbia College, still in Midtown decades before Morningside Heights, he graduates with highest honors at nineteen. The degree is a way station. His father intends Berlin next, and after Berlin the rabbinate, and the son goes to Germany carrying that intention as though it were his own.
suggested_refs: The Midtown campus of Columbia College at Forty-ninth Street and Madison Avenue

segments.name: Berlin and Heidelberg: the Doctorate and the Sermon

stops.name: Berlin, the Hochschule fur die Wissenschaft des Judenthums
stops.date_confidence: contradiction: the Jewish Encyclopedia gives 1871, which is impossible, the Hochschule having opened only in 1872 with twelve students; 1872 is the earliest attendance the calendar allows
stops.campa: In Berlin he is set to theology, philosophy and linguistics at the new College for the Science of Judaism, with philosophy and economics at the university alongside. The date the old encyclopedias give is a year too early: the school does not exist until 1872, and its roll of notable alumni does not carry his name. This pin is Berlin at large, not the Tucholskystrasse house the college occupies from 1907, thirty-five years after any lecture Adler could have sat in. He leaves the school for Heidelberg and a doctorate in philosophy.
suggested_refs: The Hochschule fur die Wissenschaft des Judentums, founded 1872
The Leo Baeck Haus, Tucholskystrasse 9, the college's home only from 1907
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Hochschule fur die Wissenschaft des Judentums' (founding year)

stops.name: Heidelberg, the doctorate summa cum laude
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day not given
stops.campa: At Heidelberg he takes his doctorate in philosophy, working in Semitics, and passes summa cum laude. Three years of German scholarship have done their work. The training his father paid for, intended to produce a second Rabbi Adler, has produced instead a young man of twenty-two who cannot say the words of the liturgy and mean them. He sails home qualified for a pulpit he no longer believes in, and expected by every person who knows him to take it within the year.
suggested_refs: The University of Heidelberg, Universitatsplatz

stops.name: Temple Emanu-El, Fifth Avenue and Forty-third Street: the sermon without God
stops.date_confidence: attested by Encyclopedia.com for 11 October 1873; the 2014 Alzey dedication speech places the same sermon in 1876, three years late, and the contradiction is left standing
stops.campa: Home from Germany, he mounts his father's pulpit and preaches once. The address, remembered as the Judaism of the future, sets aside the personal God of the prayer book and puts right conduct in its place. He never names God at all. The congregation that meant to install him as its next rabbi hears him out and declines. It is the only sermon he ever preaches there. Everything he builds afterward is built outside the synagogue and outside the church, and he never asks to be readmitted to either.
stops.quote: They compel me to do nothing which I was not previously resolved upon.
stops.quote_source: Spinoza's reply to the herem of excommunication, as given by Felix Adler in Creed and Deed (New York: G.P. Putnam's Sons, 1877), Discourse VIII: 'Spinoza'
suggested_refs: The Fifth Avenue and Forty-third Street synagogue of Temple Emanu-El, opened 1868
sources: Gerhard Holzer, dedication speech, American Ethical Union, 2014 (dissenting date)

segments.name: Ithaca, and the Lecture of May 1876

stops.name: Cornell University, Ithaca: the chair given and withdrawn
stops.date_confidence: attested for the appointment in 1874 and the end of funding in 1876; months not given
stops.campa: Endowed money brings him to Ithaca as nonresident professor of Hebrew and Oriental literature, twenty-three years old, lecturing to Christians on the Semitic scriptures. He holds the chair two years. In 1876 Cornell declines to continue the funding, the reason reported as objection to his religious views, which is the objection Emanu-El made from the other side. Neither the synagogue of his father nor a Protestant university will keep him. At twenty-four he is out of work and out of both houses at once.
stops.quote: Spinoza's name marks a lofty peak in human history. He was a true man; no man more fully lived his teachings.
stops.quote_source: Felix Adler, Creed and Deed: A Series of Discourses (New York: G.P. Putnam's Sons, 1877), Discourse VIII: 'Spinoza'
suggested_refs: The Cornell chair of Hebrew and Oriental literature, endowed and then unrenewed

stops.name: Standard Hall, New York: the lecture of the fifteenth of May
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the hall's exact site rests on the Society's own history page and is not independently confirmed
stops.campa: Invited back to New York to speak, he stands up at twenty-four and proposes a religion with no theology in it, no creed and no ritual, holding that men who will never agree about the nature of God can agree entirely about what ought to be done. He calls it Ethical Culture. Prayer is to be excluded, he says, and every form of ritual with it. The lecture is dated ever after as the beginning of the movement, though the Society itself will not be incorporated for another nine months.
stops.quote: There is a great and crying evil in modern society. It is want of purpose.
stops.quote_source: Felix Adler, Founding Address, New York Society for Ethical Culture, 15 May 1876 (American Ethical Union archival text)
suggested_refs: Standard Hall, Forty-second Street and Broadway, site of the founding address
sources: Britannica, 'Felix Adler' (inaccessible, 403 Forbidden; known via search summary only)

stops.name: New York, the Society incorporated
stops.date_confidence: attested for February 1877; the day is not given, and the pin repeats the Standard Hall coordinate for want of a documented office
stops.campa: In February the New York Society for Ethical Culture is chartered, the banker Joseph Seligman among those who help. Adler is its lecturer and stays its lecturer for fifty-six years. On Sunday mornings it does what the churches do, in rented halls, with the theology removed: an address, no prayer, and a program of work in the tenements to follow from it. The 2014 Alzey speech folds sermon, lecture and incorporation into one event of 1876 and so loses about three years.
stops.quote: not by the Creed but by the Deed.
stops.quote_source: Felix Adler, Creed and Deed: A Series of Discourses (New York: G.P. Putnam's Sons, 1877), given there as the motto of the Society
suggested_refs: The 1877 certificate of incorporation of the New York Society for Ethical Culture

segments.name: Deed, Not Creed: the Nurse, the Kindergarten, the Tenement

stops.name: Blankenburg, Thuringia: the word Adler's school inherits
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: institutional descent, not contact; Froebel dies in 1852, twenty-six years before Adler's school opens
stops.campa: Thirty-eight years before the New York school, in a Thuringian valley, Friedrich Froebel coins the word Kindergarten, a garden of children, and works out a method to go with it, on the principle that the youngest learn through their hands and not through a book. The word crosses the Atlantic before Adler uses it, and crosses again to Sarmiento's Argentina. Froebel's system rests on a graded set of wooden blocks and paper folds, the gifts, meant to teach form and number through play rather than recitation. Adler takes the method and attaches to it something Froebel did not: parents who pay nothing.
suggested_refs: Froebel's naming of the Kindergarten at Blankenburg, 1840
The Froebel gifts and their diffusion through American reform pedagogy

stops.name: The Lower East Side, the District Nursing Department
stops.date_confidence: contradiction: Wikipedia dates the founding 1877 and the Jewish Encyclopedia 1878; nothing consulted settles it, and the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: The Society's first work is a nurse sent into rooms no doctor enters: a district nursing service, trained women climbing tenement stairs with the Society's money behind them. Wikipedia gives 1877 and the Jewish Encyclopedia 1878, and no source consulted settles which is right. The department is sometimes called the seed of the Visiting Nurse Service of New York, but that descent is unsupported. The Visiting Nurse Service traces itself to Lillian Wald and Henry Street in 1893, sixteen years downstream.
suggested_refs: The District Nursing Department of the New York Society for Ethical Culture

stops.name: New York, Creed and Deed
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month is a placeholder and the pin is Manhattan at large, no source giving a place of composition
stops.campa: Putnam's issues the discourses of the first year under the title Creed and Deed. In them he takes religion apart from theology and keeps the half he wants: the feeling of the sublime, the sacredness of conduct, immortality moved out of the next world and into the effects a life leaves behind it in this one. The book is the movement's first doctrine, printed in the same year the Society is chartered. Fifty years of Sunday lecturing will elaborate it and will never replace it.
stops.quote: Religion is not identical with theology.
stops.quote_source: Felix Adler, Creed and Deed: A Series of Discourses (New York: G.P. Putnam's Sons, 1877), Discourse II: 'Religion'
suggested_refs: Creed and Deed (1877), Project Gutenberg e-text 37697
sources: Project Gutenberg 37697, Creed and Deed, full text

stops.name: New York, the first free kindergarten in the city
stops.date_confidence: the year 1878 is attested; the street is not, and the coordinate is a declared placeholder rather than a location
stops.campa: Handbills go out through the poor districts announcing a school that costs nothing, and the first free kindergarten in New York City opens with a handful of children. Two addresses have been given for it, West Sixty-fourth Street and West Forty-fourth, and no source consulted supports either; the Sixty-fourth Street figure is the Meeting House of 1910 reaching backward thirty-two years. The frequent claim that this is the first free kindergarten in the United States is false. Boston has one in 1870, St. Louis in 1873.
suggested_refs: The 1878 free kindergarten of the New York Society for Ethical Culture
Elizabeth Peabody's Boston free kindergarten, 1870; Susan Blow's St. Louis kindergarten, 1873

stops.name: Brooklyn, the marriage to Helen Goldmark
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the chronology gives Brooklyn and the geography lens gives New York City, so the pin is Brooklyn at large and the month a placeholder
stops.campa: He marries Helen Goldmark, of a Brooklyn family that will put more reformers into the Progressive decades than most cities manage: her sister Josephine works on labor law, her sister Pauline on the conditions under which women work. Five children follow, Waldo, Eleanor, Lawrence, Margaret and Ruth. The marriage ties Ethical Culture into a network of people who legislate, litigate and inspect, and it gives the movement's founder a household in which to be argued with.
suggested_refs: The Goldmark family of Brooklyn and the Progressive reform network

stops.name: New York, the Workingman's School
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1880; the month is a placeholder and the pin is Manhattan at large for want of a sourced address
stops.campa: Elementary grades are added above the kindergarten and the institution takes the name Workingman's School: academic subjects and manual training together, on the principle that the hand teaches the head and that a poor child is owed both. It is free. In 1895 it is renamed the Ethical Culture School and begins taking fee-paying pupils beside the others. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry reading 1880, established free kindergarten, is a compression of this founding, not a rival date for 1878.
suggested_refs: The Workingman's School, 1880, renamed the Ethical Culture School in 1895

stops.name: The Lower East Side, the model tenements
stops.date_confidence: attested for the company in 1885 with the building program running to 1887; the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: With others he founds the Tenement House Building Company, a limited dividend concern built on a wager: that decent housing for the poor can be raised and let and still return a modest profit, and that proving it will shame the ordinary landlord. Six buildings go up on the Lower East Side by 1887 at a cost near one hundred and fifty-five thousand dollars. This is not charity and is not offered as charity. It is a demonstration addressed to men who will not listen to any other kind of argument.
suggested_refs: The Tenement House Building Company model houses, Lower East Side, 1885 to 1887

segments.name: The Movement Travels: Halls, Journals, Summer Schools

stops.name: Parana, Argentina: the same word in another hemisphere
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Parana kindergarten; the link to Adler is parallel diffusion and no contact between him and Sarmiento's circle is documented
stops.campa: Sara Chamberlain de Eccleston opens a kindergarten at Parana six years after Adler's, under Sarmiento's schooling program and the Sociedad Froebeliana Argentina. Nothing joins the two schools but their common parent. The Froebelian free kindergarten is moving through the Atlantic world on its own momentum in these decades: Boston in 1870, St. Louis in 1873, New York in 1878, Parana in 1884. Nothing consulted records a letter passing between any of the four.
suggested_refs: The Parana normal-school kindergarten, 4 August 1884
Sociedad Froebeliana Argentina

stops.name: New York, the International Journal of Ethics
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month is a placeholder and the pin is Manhattan at large
stops.campa: He founds a scholarly quarterly for the philosophical study of conduct, the International Journal of Ethics, which outlives him and outlives its own name and is published still as Ethics. A movement of Sunday lectures and tenement nurses now has an academic organ, and the morality Adler preaches to shopkeepers is argued in the same pages where professors argue over Kant. What began as an address in a rented hall is also, from this year, a subject with a bibliography.
suggested_refs: The International Journal of Ethics, founded 1890, later Ethics

stops.name: Plymouth, Massachusetts, the Summer School of Applied Ethics
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Encyclopedia.com attests the school in 1891, but the participation of William James and John Dewey is reported rather than documented here, and the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: For several summers a school of applied ethics convenes at Plymouth, with William James and John Dewey named among those who take part. Pedagogy, economics and religion are taught for a season to teachers and ministers who carry the vocabulary home with them in September. Dewey's later school work and Adler's stand close enough that the Plymouth weeks look like a hinge, though nothing consulted traces a particular idea travelling from either man to the other.
suggested_refs: The Summer School of Applied Ethics, Plymouth, Massachusetts, from 1891

stops.name: Berlin, the German Society for Ethical Culture
stops.date_confidence: attested for the founding in 1892; no source consulted places Adler in Berlin for it, and the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: Wilhelm Foerster and Georg von Gizycki found a German Society for Ethical Culture on the New York model, and the idea spreads into Switzerland and Austria. Adler is not present. The claim made in the 2014 Alzey speech, that the young Einstein met Adler's ideas through this society during his Zurich years, is unsupported by anything consulted here; Einstein's documented association with the ethical movement is Berlin and later New York, decades further on.
stops.quote: Diversity in the creed, unanimity in the deed! This is that practical religion from which none dissents.
stops.quote_source: Felix Adler, Founding Address, New York Society for Ethical Culture, 15 May 1876 (American Ethical Union archival text)
suggested_refs: Deutsche Gesellschaft fur Ethische Kultur, founded 1892 by Wilhelm Foerster and Georg von Gizycki
sources: Gerhard Holzer, dedication speech, American Ethical Union, 2014 (the Einstein claim, rejected here)

stops.name: New York, The Moral Instruction of Children
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year against Wikipedia's works list; the month is a placeholder and the pin is Manhattan at large
stops.campa: The book that carries his teaching furthest is not addressed to philosophers. The Moral Instruction of Children sets out how to bring a child to right conduct without doctrine: fairy tales, the Hebrew scriptures read as literature, Homer and the Odyssey, graded by age, each used for the moral it carries rather than the God it names. Teachers who have never heard of Ethical Culture will work from the method. The schoolroom is where his argument actually lands.
stops.quote: The old Ideal emphasizes the Eternal that is without us; the new the Eternal that is within ourselves.
stops.quote_source: Felix Adler, Creed and Deed (New York: G.P. Putnam's Sons, 1877), Discourse III: 'The New Ideal'
suggested_refs: The Moral Instruction of Children (1892)

stops.name: Carnegie Music Hall, New York: two movements under one roof
stops.date_confidence: attested for the founding of Stebbins's school in October 1893; the Society's own progress from Standard Hall through Chickering Hall to Carnegie Hall is dated only by decade
stops.campa: Outgrowing Standard Hall and then Chickering Hall at Fifth Avenue and Eighteenth Street, the Society's Sunday meetings arrive at Carnegie Hall. In the same building in 1893 Genevieve Stebbins opens her New York School of Expression, and her roll of pupils names Felix Adler of the Ethical Society beside S. S. Curry and C. W. Emerson. The founder of a religion of conduct is learning, in his forties, how to stand and breathe and be heard from a platform.
suggested_refs: Carnegie Hall, opened 1891
New York School of Expression prospectus, 1893

stops.name: Boston, the Lowell Institute lectures
stops.date_confidence: attested for the course, given as the season 1896 to 1897; the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: The Lowell Institute gives him six public lectures on the ethics of marriage, before a Boston audience formed by Unitarian and transcendentalist habits rather than by Reform Judaism. He is now a man that other institutions invite. The vocabulary he improvised in a rented hall twenty years earlier is spoken in Boston, in Berlin, and in the four London societies federating this same year as the Union of Ethical Societies, increasingly by people who never attach his name to it.
suggested_refs: The Lowell Institute lecture course on the ethics of marriage, 1896 to 1897
The Union of Ethical Societies, London, 1896

segments.name: Columbia, and the Children in the Mills

stops.name: Columbia University, Morningside Heights: the chair of Political and Social Ethics
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: Columbia creates a chair for him in political and social ethics and he holds it thirty-one years, to the end of his life. The college that graduated him in 1870 in Midtown takes him back on its new uptown campus as professor of a subject that barely exists yet. The heterodoxy that cost him Emanu-El and cost him Cornell is now his qualification. He lectures to undergraduates in the week and to the Society on Sunday, and the two audiences hear substantially the same thing.
suggested_refs: The Columbia chair of Political and Social Ethics, created for Adler in 1902

stops.name: New York, Life and Destiny
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left standing: Encyclopedia.com gives 1903 and a Britannica-derived summary gives 1905; the month is a placeholder and the pin is Manhattan at large
stops.campa: A volume of addresses on suffering, work, marriage and death, gathered off the Sunday platform and printed for readers who will never enter the hall. Two reference works give two years for it, 1903 and 1905, and neither is preferred here over the other. The book is where his ethic touches the ordinary furniture of a life, which is where he always insisted it had to be tested: not in the metaphysics but at the deathbed, at the wage, at the table where a family is fed or is not.
stops.quote: Virtue can have no recompense, save as it is its own recompense, and vice can receive no real punishment save as it is its own avenger.
stops.quote_source: Felix Adler, Creed and Deed (New York: G.P. Putnam's Sons, 1877), Discourse I: 'Immortality'
suggested_refs: Life and Destiny (1903)
sources: Britannica-derived search summary (Britannica itself returned 403 Forbidden)

stops.name: New York, the National Child Labor Committee
stops.date_confidence: attested for the founding and the chairmanship in 1904; no source consulted gives the committee's address, so the pin is Manhattan at large and the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: He becomes founding chairman of the National Child Labor Committee and keeps the chair for a quarter of a century. The Society's instinct, go and look at how the poor actually live, hardens into a national lobby with investigators, draft statutes and a mailing list. Children in the glass houses, the cotton mills and the coal breakers are counted for the first time by people paid to count them. No source consulted gives the committee's street address, and an earlier claim pinning it to the Empire State Building site was invented.
stops.quote: not in the creed but in the deed! In the deed is the pledge of the sacredness of life; in the deed is the reward of our activities in health; in the deed our solace, and our salvation even in the abysmal gulfs of woe.
stops.quote_source: Felix Adler, Creed and Deed (New York: G.P. Putnam's Sons, 1877), Discourse VII: 'Our Consolations'
suggested_refs: The National Child Labor Committee, founded 1904

stops.name: New York, The Religion of Duty and The Essentials of Spirituality
stops.date_confidence: both titles verified to 1905 against Wikipedia's works list and OpenLibrary; the widely repeated 1908 date for The Essentials of Spirituality comes from an error in Wikipedia's prose and is rejected here
stops.campa: Two short books in one year: the first on duty as the entire content of religion, the second on what is left of spirituality once the supernatural has been taken out of it. He is fifty-four and the doctrine has set into its final shape. The worth of a person is not conferred by God and not derived from usefulness; it comes from the place each one holds in a whole that is made of others and could not be made without them. Reference works have been misdating these two for a century.
stops.quote: The feeling of the sublime is the root of the religious sentiment.
stops.quote_source: Felix Adler, Creed and Deed (New York: G.P. Putnam's Sons, 1877), Discourse II: 'Religion'
suggested_refs: The Religion of Duty (1905)
The Essentials of Spirituality (New York: James Pott and Co., 1905)

stops.name: Berlin, the Theodore Roosevelt Chair
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left standing: the JTA obituary gives the Berlin exchange professorship as 1908, the 2014 Alzey speech as 1909; the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: He returns to Berlin as exchange professor, holding the Theodore Roosevelt Chair of American History and Institutions: the boy who left Alzey at five, sent back to explain America to the Germans. Thirty-six years before, he had sat in this city as a rabbinical student who could not believe what he was being trained to preach. The sources disagree by one year over when the chair was held, 1908 by one account and 1909 by another, and neither is preferred here over the other.
suggested_refs: The Theodore Roosevelt Chair of American History and Institutions, University of Berlin
sources: Gerhard Holzer, dedication speech, American Ethical Union, 2014 (dissenting year)

stops.name: New York, the Committee hires Lewis Hine
stops.date_confidence: attested for the hiring in 1908; the month is a placeholder and the pin is Manhattan at large for want of a sourced address
stops.campa: The National Child Labor Committee puts a schoolteacher with a camera on its payroll. Lewis Hine walks into the mills with a notebook of pretexts, measures children against the buttons of his own coat to estimate their height, and photographs them standing at the spinning frames and squatting over the coal chutes. The prints go out over the Committee's name, and legislators who will not read a report look at a photograph of a six-year-old at a machine.
suggested_refs: Lewis Hine's National Child Labor Committee photographs, 1908 onward

stops.name: Two West Sixty-fourth Street: the Meeting House
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month is a placeholder, and the coordinate is the canonical atlas pin for this building, inherited unchanged
stops.campa: After thirty-four years of rented rooms the Society builds. Robert D. Kohn raises a meeting house at Sixty-fourth Street and Central Park West in a Viennese Secession idiom, the facade later landmarked, with the school beside it. It is a church in every respect but the one that matters to Adler: nothing inside it is addressed to God. The building will hold his funeral. From the following autumn it holds, in a classroom, a seven-year-old whose name the century learns later.
suggested_refs: The Ethical Culture Meeting House, 2 West 64th Street, Robert D. Kohn, 1910
The landmarked Secessionist facade on Central Park West

segments.name: The Bureau, the Lectures, and the Last Books

stops.name: The Ethical Culture School, Central Park West: a boy of seven enters
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In September a physics-minded seven-year-old from Riverside Drive is enrolled in Adler's school: Robert Oppenheimer, who will spend eleven years under the motto deed before creed and leave it, by the account of everyone who knew him, with a conscience formed and no religion to keep it in. Ethics is a subject in the timetable here, taught like arithmetic. Adler is sixty and still lecturing. What the conscience of an Ethical Culture boy is worth gets tested at Los Alamos, thirty-four years on.
stops.quote_source: Motto of the New York Society for Ethical Culture (Felix Adler)
suggested_refs: The Ethical Culture School, 33 Central Park West
Bird and Sherwin, American Prometheus, chapters 1 to 2

stops.name: New York, the executive board of the National Urban League
stops.date_confidence: the board membership is attested; no source consulted gives the year he joined, and this date marks the League's own founding year as a declared placeholder
stops.campa: He sits on the first executive board of the National Urban League, which works on the housing, employment and welfare of black families arriving in the northern cities. The Ethical Culture pattern repeats itself: a Sunday morning argument, then a committee, then an institution with a staff and a budget. What year he joined the board is given nowhere in the sources consulted, and the date attached to this stop should be read as an admission of that rather than as a fact.
suggested_refs: The first executive board of the National Urban League

stops.name: New York, the Civil Liberties Bureau
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month is a placeholder and the pin is Manhattan at large
stops.campa: In the first year of American belligerence he serves on the Civil Liberties Bureau, the wartime body defending conscientious objectors and dissenters against a government prosecuting speech. He is sixty-six years old. The organization becomes the American Civil Liberties Union three years later. A man who lost a pulpit and lost a professorship for what he thought spends the war holding open the same door for other people, most of whom think nothing he thinks.
suggested_refs: The Civil Liberties Bureau, 1917, forerunner of the American Civil Liberties Union

stops.name: New York, An Ethical Philosophy of Life
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month is a placeholder and the pin is Manhattan at large
stops.campa: At sixty-seven he sets the system out whole: the worth of every person as an end and never as a means, argued not from Kant's law alone but from what he calls the ethical manifold, in which the distinctness of each person is the thing that makes the whole possible. It is his most sustained book and his least read. The movement runs on the sentences of 1876; the philosophy underneath them arrives forty-two years late, and arrives mostly to professionals.
stops.quote: Where the roots of private virtue are diseased, the fruit of public probity cannot but be corrupt.
stops.quote_source: Felix Adler, Founding Address, New York Society for Ethical Culture, 15 May 1876 (American Ethical Union archival text)
suggested_refs: An Ethical Philosophy of Life (1918)

stops.name: Manchester College, Oxford: the Hibbert Lectures
stops.date_confidence: attested for May 1923 at Manchester College rather than the university at large; the day is not given, and the JTA obituary's claim that these lectures were published as An Ethical Philosophy of Life is wrong, that book having appeared in 1918
stops.campa: In May he delivers the Hibbert Lectures at Manchester College in Oxford, seventy-one years old, an American nontheist addressing an English dissenting foundation on what a spiritual ideal can be rebuilt out of. They go into print as The Reconstruction of the Spiritual Ideal, whose title page names the college and the month. Wikipedia's works list dates the first edition 1923 and OpenLibrary 1924. The figure of 1925 in circulation has no edition standing behind it.
suggested_refs: The Reconstruction of the Spiritual Ideal: Hibbert Lectures Delivered in Manchester College, Oxford, May 1923 (D. Appleton and Co., OCLC 607376)

stops.name: Riverdale, the Bronx: the Fieldston campus
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: Fifty years after a handful of children in a rented room, the school opens a hilltop campus in Riverdale and takes the name Fieldston. The lower school stays on Central Park West. The institution that began as an argument about what the children of the poor are owed becomes, and remains, one of the most expensive private schools in the United States, teaching ethics in the timetable to the grandchildren of the people Adler was lecturing at on Sunday mornings.
suggested_refs: The Fieldston campus, Riverdale, opened 1928

stops.name: New York, the Eastern Division of the American Philosophical Association
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month is a placeholder and the pin is Manhattan at large
stops.campa: The philosophers elect him president of their eastern division. He is seventy-seven. A discipline with no obvious place for a lecturer who has no church, no denomination and no metaphysics it recognizes puts him in its chair for the year. He has outlasted every institution that turned him out, Emanu-El and Cornell both, and he has done it without once asking either of them to reconsider, and without founding anything that could turn anybody out in its turn.
suggested_refs: The presidency of the Eastern Division of the American Philosophical Association, 1928

stops.name: Mount Sinai Hospital, New York: the death
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: An operation for an intestinal illness in 1932 leaves him weakened, and a year later he dies at Mount Sinai Hospital at eighty-one, still holding the Columbia chair and still lecturing to the Society. His death has sometimes been placed only loosely on the Upper West Side, but the obituary filed by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency two days afterward names the hospital plainly, and the record can be fixed to the building rather than left as a hedge.
suggested_refs: Mount Sinai Hospital, Fifth Avenue and 100th Street
sources: Jewish Telegraphic Agency, 'Dr. Felix Adler, Noted Educator, Founder of Ethical Culture, Dead', 26 April 1933

stops.name: Two West Sixty-fourth Street: the funeral
stops.date_confidence: attested: the obituary gives the funeral as Thursday at ten in the morning from the Meeting House, and the Thursday following Monday 24 April 1933 is the twenty-seventh
stops.campa: They carry him into the meeting house he built, and John Elliott and David Muzzey speak over him: no prayer, no liturgy, no committal to any God, by the rule he laid down in 1876 and never once relaxed. It is the same building where, eight years earlier, a Riverside Drive boy named Robert Oppenheimer had begun eleven years of schooling in ethics without creed. Records of the building's exact coordinates have disagreed by up to a quarter of a mile over the years; the figure used here is the address of the Central Park West building itself, so that one address keeps one place.
stops.quote: We propose to entirely exclude prayer and every form of ritual.
stops.quote_source: Felix Adler, Founding Address, New York Society for Ethical Culture, 15 May 1876 (American Ethical Union archival text)
suggested_refs: The Meeting House of the New York Society for Ethical Culture, 2 West 64th Street

stops.name: Mount Pleasant Cemetery, Hawthorne: the uncut boulder
stops.date_confidence: the burial and the cemetery are attested; the day is inferred from the funeral, and the uncut-boulder marker rests on a 2014 dedication text at aeu.org that now returns 404 and could not be re-read
stops.campa: He is buried in a nonsectarian ground in Westchester under a large uncut boulder: no cross on it, no star, nothing carved that belongs to anybody's revelation. Coordinates recorded for this cemetery elsewhere have not been reliable; the figure used here follows OpenStreetMap. The grandfather lies at Worms in the Rabbinental under Hebrew letters, among rabbis. The grandson lies under a stone that has been left exactly as the glacier left it.
suggested_refs: Mount Pleasant Cemetery, Hawthorne, New York

stops.name: Germany and Austria: the societies banned
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the source dates the suppression only to 1933 and after, and the month here is a placeholder
stops.campa: In the year of his death the National Socialists take power and the ethical societies of Germany and Austria are shut. The movement born in a New York hall and carried back to Berlin by Foerster and Gizycki is suppressed in the country Adler was born in, and its members scatter or go quiet. He is two months dead and does not see it. The American societies continue, and continue still, keeping the Sunday platform, the tenement work, and the schools he fastened to them.
suggested_refs: The suppression of the German and Austrian ethical societies after 1933

stops.name: Alzey, the bronze relief on the birth house
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the dedication is described in a 2014 American Ethical Union text at aeu.org that now returns 404 and could not be re-read for confirmation
stops.campa: Eighty-one years after his death a bronze relief is fixed to the corner house at Schlossgasse and Amtsgasse, the second Adler plaque in the town, his father's standing already on Hospitalstrasse. The speaker at the dedication says plainly why the thing is needed: in Alzey, Felix Adler is scarcely known. A man founds a religion, a school system and a national campaign against the labor of children in one country, and leaves in the street where he was born a hole that has to be filled with a plaque.
suggested_refs: The 2014 bronze relief on Adler's birth house, Alzey
